body.objective: Students will be able to compare work to quality standards.
body.iCan: I can compare work to quality standards.
successCriteria: I can compare my work to a written standard or specification
I can conduct a structured peer review
I can find defects, identify causes and revise
body.hook: Restaurant inspectors, building inspectors and quality control technicians all do the same thing: compare work to a standard. In intermediate CTS, you start working to standards like a professional and helping peers do the same.

vocabulary.definition: An agreed level of quality that work must meet.

study.title: Inspect and Improve
study.question: How do professionals check work against standards and improve it?
study.passage:
Part 1, Read the spec (10 minutes): Use the specification for your project. Examples:
• Foods: Food safety standard: internal temperature of chicken at least 74 °C; plating within 5 minutes; portion 150 g ± 10 g.
• Construction: Joints flush within 0.5 mm; diagonals within 2 mm (proves square); no visible glue.
• Fashion: Seam allowance 1.5 cm; stitches 2.5 mm; no puckering; finished size ± 1 cm.
• Computing: Page loads under 3 seconds; works on phone and desktop; all links work; alt text on images.
Part 2, Inspection checklist (10 minutes): Turn the spec into a yes or no checklist with a measurement column.
Part 3, Peer inspection (15 minutes): Swap projects. Inspect with the checklist. Record measurements, not opinions.
Part 4, Root cause (10 minutes): For each defect, ask "Why?" up to five times to find the root cause (the "5 Whys").
Part 5, Revise (15 minutes): Fix what can be fixed. For what can't, write a process change for next time.
study.source: Original quality task written for this lesson; the 5 Whys is a common quality improvement method.

examples.title: Specification
examples.problem: Diagonals of a box measure 402 mm and 405 mm. Spec: within 2 mm. Pass?
examples.answer: Fail; the box is not square

examples.title: Food standard
examples.problem: Chicken reads 68 °C. Spec: at least 74 °C. What do you do?
examples.explore: Why is this a safety issue?

examples.title: 5 Whys
examples.problem: Seam puckered. Why? Tension too tight. Why? Machine settings changed. Why? Not checked. Root cause?
examples.answer: Root cause: no setup check before sewing

examples.title: Peer review
examples.problem: Turn "the website looks broken" into an inspection note.
examples.answer: Link 3 returns a 404 error; spec requires all links to work
examples.explore: How would you test all links?

practice.q: Portion spec 150 g ± 10 g. Is 162 g acceptable?
practice.a: No, the range is 140 to 160 g.

practice.q: Why measure diagonals of a box?
practice.a: Equal diagonals prove it is square.

practice.q: Why record measurements in peer review?
practice.a: They are objective and show exactly what to fix.

practice.q: What is the minimum safe internal temperature for chicken?
What's the difference between fixing and preventing a defect?
practice.a: Fixing repairs one product; preventing changes the process so it doesn't happen again.

practice.q: Why do industries use written standards?
How should a reviewer give feedback on a failed spec?
practice.a: State the spec, the measurement and the result, respectfully.

practice.q: Why might a product meet the spec but still disappoint a user?
practice.a: The spec may not include everything the user needs.

misconceptions: Thinking peer review means saying whether you like it
Fixing the symptom without finding the cause
